paper_title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models has recently helped scale capabilities in domains such as software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), computer use (Hu et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024), and scientific discovery (Xu et al., 2026). Wider access to open-source training environments (Jain et al., 2025; Qiang et al., 2025) has aided this progress. Yet sandboxes that stay stable when training is scaled up are still hard to engineer. Recent work has shown that language models can approximate realistic world behavior and, when used as simulators, improve downstream results (Li et al., 2026; Deshpande, 2026; Zuo et al., 2026). However, evaluating these world models as general-purpose simulators remains difficult, because good metrics are poorly understood and no benchmark attributes failures to specific simulation capabilities. If simulator is wrong in ways that an agent can exploit, RL optimizes against those mistakes instead of the real environment dynamics. To locate where these models fail, we first propose two taxonomies for world-model evaluation. One has four core capabilities, and the other has 19 skills (Figure 1). skill is specific behavior of the environment, such as remembering value that was written many turns earlier. Appendix A.1 gives definitions, counts, axes, and mappings of these skills. From these taxonomies we build GLOBEBENCH, benchmark of 1,632 multi-turn traces from code, enterprise tool use, games, math and science, and dialogue environments. Each item tests one skill and pairs trajectory and final action with the gold next state, which we obtain deterministically by executing the action in the items backend. Each item is also labeled, where applicable, with its reach-back and impact radius, which we define in Section 3. Every item passes 12 automatic quality gates that check that the answer is consistent with the visible history, that the gold is reproducible, and that the item is unambiguous, and not duplicate (Appendix A.5). To assess the quality of the dataset, we combine human study of 200 items with an LLM-judge audit. 1 Figure 1: The 19 primary skills in one shared library database. Each card pairs an action (top) with the response faithful environment returns (bottom). GLOBEBENCH items test the same behaviors, but the state that decides the outcome is usually set many turns earlier. When we score responses, deterministic gates settle only those predictions that provably match or contradict the gold, and we delegate the rest, which require judgment, to an LLM judge. Whether automated judgments of this kind track human ones is untested, so we study it here. In this study we investigate the following research questions: RQ1 Which parts of predicted next state do models get wrong, and do open-weight and closed models fail in the same way? RQ2 Do text world models exhibit recurring failure modes that aggregate task success rates leave undetected? RQ3 How well do automated judgments align with human qualitative judgments of model outputs, and where do the two diverge? We release GLOBEBENCH, 1,632-item benchmark spanning five domains whose golds come from execution rather than annotation, together with hybrid grader that settles deterministically whatever it can and defers the remainder to an LLM judge. response can look right and still carry the wrong numbers, so we score whether the state is correct rather than whether the answer resembles one. Under this grader, no model solves even half the benchmark. An aggregate success rate also hides where the failures sit and the leading models margin comes almost entirely from items the rest never solve which tells us where the difficulty lies. Our automated judge agrees with the human annotators on most rubric dimensions and is stricter on whether state stays consistent with its history. We release the benchmark, evaluation harness, model outputs, judge records, and reproduction instructions at https://github.com/patronus-ai/globebench, and the items and model results at https://huggingface.co/datasets/PatronusAI/globebench.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Language world models for agents. Li et al. (2026) evaluate text world models on fidelity and consistency, scaling and robustness, and utility for downstream agents. They find that usefulness depends on behavioral coverage and environment complexity. Deshpande (2026) frames text world modeling as predicting steerable transitions from an initial state, task context, tool schema, domain rules, and steering directives while comparing output state diversity produced by autoregressive and masked-diffusion models. Zuo et al. (2026) train Qwen-AgentWorld across seven agent domains and release it with AgentWorldBench, which pairs predicted observations with real execution outputs. 2 Executable agent environments. Several GLOBEBENCH trajectories come from executable testbeds: stateful multi-turn tool use from the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (Patil et al., 2025), text games generated by TextWorld (Côté et al., 2018), and conversations from τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) in which both the user and the agent use tools. Symbolic backends such as SymPy (Meurer et al., 2017) give reproducible next states. We use these systems as trajectory sources or execution backends, and we evaluate models that predict their behavior rather than agents that act in them. Evaluation of simulation fidelity. AgentWorldBench (Zuo et al., 2026) is the closest prior evaluation. It grades predicted observations on five rubric dimensions: format, factuality, consistency, realism, and quality (completeness and conciseness against the reference). EnvSimBench (Liu et al., 2026) also benchmarks LLM-based environment simulation, and it scores the text that an environment returns to the agent separately from the resulting state change. Its analysis covers format mismatches and hallucinated transitions, including cases where the simulator invents constraint violation and blocks an action the real environment would have accepted. GLOBEBENCH differs in what single item is. Prior benchmarks score predicted observation as whole, whereas each GLOBEBENCH item is constructed to isolate one skill. Quality gates discard any item that can be solved without exercising it. failure therefore points to the mechanism that the item tests. We additionally record each items reach-back and impact radius, the two axes along which we expect difficulty to vary, and report results along both (Section 6.1).

sections.title: 3 GLOBEBENCH CURATION
sections.content: Items. Each item is tuple = (P, a, g, m), where = (τ1, . . . , τH ) is the collection of visible turns of the interaction (earlier actions and the environments responses) before the final action, is the final action, is the next state, and the metadata holds how the item was made and what it tests. We obtain by executing against backend (fixed software environment). The backend is either container image, identified by its digest. We have fixed backend because the gold has to stay fixed target. Without that, the backend could drift and mismatch between the correct prediction and the gold can occur. The model under evaluation sees only and a: ˆg = fθ(P, a), (1) and ˆg is scored against g, which the model never observes. Capability and skill taxonomies. We introduce the terms Capabilities and Skills. capability is broad behavior that world model must show, and skill is one specific behavior of the environment that an item tests. Each skill can map to one or more capabilities. Prior evaluations organize judgments by rubric dimension (Zuo et al., 2026) or failure type (Liu et al., 2026), whereas we organize them by the environment behavior that an item is built to test. We define four capabilities that subsume the dimensions prior evaluations score (Zuo et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026) while keeping each tied to an environment behavior. State Coherence requires predictions to stay consistent with established entities and facts in the prior context. Causal Correctness requires the predicted next state to reflect what the action actually does, so that distinct actions and histories yield correct, distinct next states and side effects. Interface Fidelity requires predictions to match the real systems output, including the same fields, keys, and error classes. Constraint Enforcement requires that valid actions execute and that actions violating an established constraint be refused. Interface fidelity governs what that refusal should look like. Each item tests one primary skill. Items may also carry additional capability and failure labels. Domains and sources. The corpus contains 526 Code, 381 Enterprise, 334 Games, 198 Math and Science, and 193 Dialogue items. Domains are not balanced by design but are generated based on the number of backends available. Of the 1,632 items, we generate 1,137 by designing the trajectory ourselves, and 955 of these run on simulators in our harness that implement rules we wrote (Appendix A.2). We choose which entities appear, which actions are taken, and in what order (Appendix A.3; Table 6 lists the backends). The remaining 495 items are adapted mainly from different open-source backends that are executable, almost all permissively licensed  (Table 7)  , and cover different transition surfaces, such as BFCL (Patil et al., 2025), TextWorld, τ 2-bench, and SymPy. 3 Trajectory construction. An operator is skeleton that builds trajectory. Each operator targets one skill and fixes the sequence of action types. These are the basic blocks that skill needs in order to be established and queried, such as writes, reads, deletes, and permission changes. Some actions are also domain-specific, such as SQL statements, shell commands, and game moves, and are fixed by the backend environment. An operator can also add filler actions that leave the tested state alone. Fillers are how we vary the reach-back distance. Some operators write trajectory from scratch, while others inject controlled change into one adapted from an open-source testbed. Either way, we execute the final action against the fixed backend (Appendix A.3). Reach-back and impact radius. We record two properties of each item (32 items have no reachback and 11 have no radius). Reach-back measures how far back the deciding evidence lies, and impact radius how far the actions effects reach. They correspond to the two directions in which model that tracks state can fail: backward through the history and outward through the state. Reach-back is the number of turns between the final action and the earlier event that its answer depends on. For probe items we count from the last event that supports the answer, so visible filler turns add to it. For synthetic long-horizon audits we instead count from the earliest event the answer depends on. Since that event is often the first action in the prefix, their reach-back is close to the trajectory length. Appendix A.3 defines both kinds of item. Impact radius describes how far the actions state change reaches. At L0 the action changes no state, so only its returned output must be predicted. At L1 and L2 it changes only entities that it names (one at L1, two or more at L2), whereas at L3 it changes at least one entity that it does not name. For 953 of the 977 L3 items, the operator that built the item declares the level instead of an execution diff measuring it, and 945 of these 953 are synthetic long-horizon audits, which are L3 by construction (Appendix A.4). Since each operator largely fixes both reach-back and radius, we use them to describe slices of the data rather than as controlled variables (Section 6.1). Quality gates. To decide whether an item can be scored, we apply 12 quality gates, which are separate from the scoring of responses. Each gate rules out one way an item could fail to measure what we intend. Deterministic gates check that the facts the answer needs are visible, the effect is observable, the gold is nonempty and reproducible, and paired actions give different answers when intended. An LLM judge checks whether each item is solvable from the visible state and unambiguous, and whether an obvious cue gives away the injected change. Six human annotators then audited 200 of the items that pass. All six rated the same 80 items, which we use to measure agreement, and the remaining 120 were divided among them. The 80 shared items cover all five domains and all 19 skills but include few long-horizon audits (Appendix C.1). Each item was rated on four dimensions: State Coherence, Interface Realism, Constraint Enforcement, and Outcome Correctness (Section 5). We extend the same rubric to the full benchmark with an LLM judge, which returned complete ratings for 1,627 of the 1,632 items (Appendix C.2).

sections.title: 4 EVALUATION SETUP
sections.content: Models. We evaluate 18 general-purpose LLMs as zero-shot text world models: Claude Fable 5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026a;b;c;d;e), Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), GLM 5.3 (Z.ai, 2026), GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a;b;c;d), Grok 4.6 (SpaceXAI, 2026), Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026), Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI, 2026), Laguna S2.1 (Poolside, 2026), Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (Qwen Team, 2026), and Qwen 3.8 Max (Alibaba Group, 2026). We also evaluate two specialized text world models, Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B (Qwen-AgentWorld) from the Qwen team (Zuo et al., 2026) and the Digital World Model (DWM) from Patronus AI (Patronus AI, 2026). We send each model one primary request per item and run each general-purpose LLM at its providers high reasoning setting (Appendix B.1). Serving and refusals. Model responses are stochastic and the served models change over time, so reproducibility here means that every reported score can be recomputed from the released outputs. Of the 32,640 model-item pairs, 28,854 have usable answer. The other 3,786 include 3,696 provider refusals by four Claude models. The remaining 90 returned no usable answer. sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: Overall performance. Table 1 shows binary task success. The top four models are GPT-6 Astra (49.57%), Grok 4.6 (28.13%), Claude Opus 5.5 (26.35%), and Qwen 3.8 Max (25.31%). Claude Opus 5.5 ranks third even though it refuses 41.36% of the items. Nearly all refusals come from Anthropics safeguards, which block requests that could enable cyber harm, such as malware, and can also block benign cybersecurity work (Anthropic, 2026f;g). The specialized text world models rank 15th (Qwen-AgentWorld, 14.46%) and 19th (DWM, 5.21%). Qwen-AgentWorld is below the median of the 18 general-purpose LLMs on 14 of the 19 skills, and DWM is below it on all 19 (Appendix D.8). Success is highest in Games (27.8%) and Enterprise (25.5%) and lowest in Math and Science (11.7%) and Dialogue (11.8%), largely in line with each domains share of L3 items (Appendix D.5). RQ1: Which parts of predicted next state do models get wrong, and do open-weight and closed models fail in the same way? Most failures report wrong value. Table 2 sorts the 22,431 answered failures by what the deterministic comparison finds in the predicted state: at least one field that contradicts the gold (wrong value), only missing or unsupported fields (structure only), or no state fields to compare, in which case the grader checks the answer as prose or by error type. Over all 20 models the three shares are 53.21%, 22.95%, and 23.84% (Appendix D.7). Open-weight models more often get value wrong (58.22% of their answered failures against 47.69% for closed models, difference of 10.53 points, 95% CI 9.04 to 12.14), and closed models more often omit or add fields (31.54% against 16.27%). The gap holds within the 1,521 items that both groups fail (55.15% against 45.92%). Closed models also give no usable response on 19.33% of their decisions, almost all through Claude refusals, while the open-weight models miss one of 9,792. sections.title: 6 ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS
sections.content: 6.1 QUANTITATIVE RESULTS Skill profiles. The 19 skills have six distinct leaders (Figure 2 and Appendix Figure 8). GPT-6 Astra leads 11 of them, including 7 of the 9 hardest, and we examine why in Section 6.2. Of the other eight, Qwen 3.8 Max leads three, Claude Opus 5.5 two, and Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Grok 4.6 one each, although Grok 4.6 shares its lead on Rule Enforcement with two other models (Appendix D.4). Solvability is not merely asserted by our gates: at least one model recovers the executed answer on 1,001 of the 1,632 items, and on seven skills every item is solved by some model. All 20 models solve only 4 items (Appendix Table 19). The 631 items that no model solves are mostly L3 (87.6%) and beyond 40 turns of reach-back (93.7%), and 85.1% come from six skills (Appendix Table 20). 7 Figure 4: Long horizon: task success by reach-back in right-closed 200-turn bins labeled by their upper edge, for 11 of the 20 models and the 20-model mean. Items per bin: 764, 195, 151, 137, 129, 133, 19, 45, 27 (Appendix Table 16). Beyond 600 turns GPT-6 Astras curve rises again, whereas the pooled rate of the other 19 models stays at or below 8.31% in every bin beyond 400 turns. Appendix D.2 relates Astras rise to the mix of operators in those bins. Impact radius and reach-back. world model has to carry state both across the entities that an action affects and across long stretches of the trajectory. On GLOBEBENCH, models lose accuracy along both axes, which we measure with impact radius and reach-back. Accuracy is highest at L0 and lowest at L3 (Figure 3). Mean success is 43.49% at L0, where nothing should change. It is nearly the same at L1 (27.12%) and L2 (27.54%), where only entities that the action names should change, and falls to 5.10% at L3, where unnamed entities should also change. Models may give plausible value for named entity but fail to update the entities that depend on it. However, almost all L3 items are synthetic long-horizon audits, which are L3 by construction (Section 3), and we read examples of them in Section 6.2. Every model does worse beyond 40 turns of reach-back than within 40 turns, and pooled success falls from 42.3% to 11.4% (Appendix D.1). Five skills (Access Control, Schema Conformance, Read and Write Persistence, Computational Accuracy, and Contradiction Detection) make up 823 of the 1,192 items beyond 40 turns, and their pooled success there ranges from 4.5% to 11.2%. In the longer bins of Figure 4, GPT-6 Astras curve rises again, whereas the pooled rate of the other 19 models stays at or below 8.31% in every bin beyond 400 turns. The rise is consistent with the mix of operators in those bins rather than with distance (Appendix D.2). Reach-back is strongly associated with primary skill (Figure 5). The correlation ratio η, which is 0 when skill says nothing about reach-back and 1 when skill determines it, is 0.69, and Cramérs between skill and reach-back quartile, on the same scale, is 0.54. We next test whether the skill mix explains the reach-back drop. If skills alone explained the drop, comparing items with shorter reach-back (at most 40 turns of reach-back) with longer ones within the same skill would remove the gap. Instead, the gap shrinks only from 30.84 to 25.11 points (Appendix Table 17), because in nine skills the short items are local probes while the long items are audits with long outputs. The gap disappears when we compare items from the same operator (+1.76 points, 95% CI 1.57 to 5.17) or items that share both skill and radius (2.20, 5.31 to 0.92). However, the comparison within operators rests on the 307 items with longer reach-back that share an operator with shorter ones. Nearly all of them lie within 301 turns, and the audits of 720 to 1,680 turns have no short items to compare with. The drop is concentrated in L3 items, where success is about 40% on the 14 short items but about 4% on the long ones. L0 items show no drop (42.6% short vs. 45.7% long). GPT-6 Astra passes 34.29% of L3 items and 40.52% of items beyond 40 turns, while the next best model on both, Claude Opus 5.5, passes 8.39% and 16.36% (Appendix Table 15). 8 Figure 5: Reach-back by primary skill (log scale): quartile boxes, median marked, 1.5IQR whiskers, jittered items, color by median. Side-Effect Propagation (32 items) has no reach-back and is not shown. Reach-back and skill are confounded by construction: the median reach-back is 11 turns for Format Stability, Temporal Ordering, and Referential Integrity, and 720 to 960 turns for Computational Accuracy, Access Control, and Error Fidelity. 6.2 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS Where GPT-6 Astras lead comes from. We read 22 items and find that the models differ mostly in the hidden state they track rather than in how they apply the rules. Most of GPT-6 Astras lead over Grok 4.6 comes from long L3 audits that depend on such state (Appendix D.10). One of them is the weighted-quorum audit alquorum1-api-s22020000-injected (Enterprise, L3). Box 1 in Appendix D.9 shows it verbatim, and its gold and all 20 models answers are in the release. Its final action audits requests to change the lifecycle state of resources. request is allowed only if its sponsors weighted votes reach threshold and the resource is in the state that the request expects. The weights and the state are computed from the resources capability by formulas stated in the first action, 720 turns before the final action. The capability is set or changed 49 times in between, but the trajectory never prints it. On the first request, Astra derives the true value, 89, reproduces the weights (1/3/1, total 5), and allows the request. Grok 4.6 applies the same formulas to capability of 262. Its weights (4/1/4), its state suspended, and its stale_state denial all follow correctly from 262, so the error lies in the tracked state rather than in the arithmetic. Astra fails 20 of the 76 audits of this kind. Failure patterns across models. Claude Opus 5.5 returns parseable JSON on 80% of the JSON items it answers, and GPT-6 Sol on 73%. Most of their other answers are prose declines or JSON wrapped in Markdown fences. In contrast, GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.6, Qwen 3.8 Max, GPT-5.5, and GPT5.6 Sol reach 99% or more, so their failures are mostly well-formed answers that report wrong state. In one game whose earlier turns used up crafting quota, Qwen 3.8 Max predicted Crafted one charge for banana (2/2), whereas the game returned banana is full; crafting quota exceeded. The prediction is plausible for the final action alone but ignores limit set eleven turns earlier (Appendix D.11). Specialized text world models. Qwen-AgentWorld beats the median of the 18 general-purpose LLMs on 5 of the 19 skills, and DWM on none. One of the five is Side-Effect Propagation, where Qwen-AgentWorld passes 15 of 32 items. However, the 95% interval of its margin over the median includes zero (Appendix D.8), and when we read those items, we find no side-effect behavior specific to it. Qwen-AgentWorld trails GPT-6 Astra by 35 points. We do not evaluate its base model, so these results do not show how much its training on next-observation prediction changed its accuracy.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced GLOBEBENCH, benchmark of 1,632 items for text world models in five domains, organized by four capabilities and 19 skills. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, solves 49.57% of the items, and 631 items are solved by none of the 20 models. Accuracy is lowest where an actions effects reach dependent objects or where reach-back exceeds 40 turns, mostly in long audits that require tracking hidden state. Many failures are well-formed but report the wrong state. Because every gold comes from execution and the grader calls semantic judge only when deterministic gates cannot decide, GLOBEBENCH shows where simulator departs from its environment. However, each item tests only one transition after fixed prefix, so we do not measure how simulators own errors compound over rollout. Task success is also binary over the whole next state, so long audit fails if any single value is wrong. Finally, since reach-back and impact radius largely follow the skill families that produced each item (Section 3), they locate hard item families without showing that distance or breadth causes the errors. We hope GLOBEBENCH will lead to more reliable evaluation of text world models and to better training signals.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Under the authors direction, we used generative AI tools, namely LLM coding agents (Claude Code with Claude models and, earlier, Codex with GPT models). We used them to implement code for the data pipeline, evaluation harness, and analyses, and to write the seeded operators that produce the synthetic items, including their templates and filler turns. They also assisted in analyzing and interpreting results, including the sample-level analysis in Section 6.2, and suggested additional analyses. Every gold next state was obtained by executing the action against pinned backend, and none was produced by an LLM. We did not use AI to propose or refine hypotheses, to develop the capability and skill taxonomies, or to clean or reformat datasets. Mathematical claims, proofs, and translation do not apply to this work. We reviewed all AI-assisted work. We also recomputed every reported number from the saved outputs with tested scripts, and we checked citations against their sources. We take responsibility for the final content, including anything produced with AI. ETHICS STATEMENT GLOBEBENCH measures how faithfully language models simulate code, enterprise, game, math, and dialogue environments. We built its items either from our own recipes or by adapting interfaces and trajectories from public sources such as BFCL, TextWorld, τ 2-bench, and SymPy. The release records the source and license of every item (Appendix A.2). In addition to the quality gates, every released item passes an automated screen for personal data, which rejects real e-mail addresses, personal account identifiers, and credential-like strings. For the human audit, we recruited six annotators through Upwork to rate 200 items, and we checked these items for personally identifying, sensitive, and harmful content (Appendix C.1). The main risk we see is misplaced trust in simulator. If simulator is wrong in ways that an agent can exploit, it trains the agent against those mistakes (Section 1). We built GLOBEBENCH to expose such errors. However, since each item tests one transition after fixed prefix and the items come from five domains, high score does not show that simulator is reliable for training (Section 7). REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We release the benchmark items, evaluation harness, and reproduction instructions at https: //github.com/patronus-ai/globebench, and the items and per-model results at https: //huggingface.co/datasets/PatronusAI/globebench. The GitHub release also includes the model outputs and judge records, so the results can be rescored without querying the models again. Section 3 and Appendix describe the pinned backends and how the items were constructed. Appendix A.2 gives the provenance record of each item, and Appendix A.5 lists the quality gates. Section 4 and Appendix describe the models we evaluated and their reasoning, routing, and sampling settings. The same sections also explain how we handle refusals and how the hybrid grader works, and they give the judge configuration and prompts. Appendix contains the annotation 10 guidelines, the rubric, and the procedure for the LLM audit. Finally, Appendix defines the pooled rates, the rounding, and the bootstrap intervals behind the reported results.

It names the backend and the kinds of entities the environment contains. It also names the numeric parameters of trajectory and the actions that the domain allows. The recipes written for domain determine which skills that domain can test. An operator sets the order of actions in trajectory. It is list of steps, and each step adds one or more actions. Steps include writing, reading, or deleting an object, changing permission, and adding to quota. Each pairing of recipe and an operator has fixed string identifier. We draw the objects, entities, facts, and numeric values from independent random streams, so trajectories vary while the skill under test stays the same. There are two kinds of operators. Some simulate whole trajectory from fixed random seed. Others take trajectory adapted from an open-source testbed and inject controlled change into it. Both kinds inject changes and execute the final action against the backend in the same way. An operator can also add filler actions, such as reading an unrelated file or record. filler action touches no object that the tested skill depends on. We add filler only to control how many turns separate the evidence from the final action. We count reach-back differently for probe items and for synthetic long-horizon audits. In probe item, the final action checks one piece of state that an earlier event set, as when it reads value written earlier or acts after permission was revoked. We count its reach-back from the last event in the prefix that supports the answer. synthetic long-horizon audit is an item with long generated trajectory whose final action asks for long output that depends on state set throughout the trajectory, such as the weighted-quorum audit in Appendix D.9. We count its reach-back from the earliest event that the answer depends on. In several audits this event is the first action of the prefix, so reach-back equals the length of the prefix minus one. For the audits, reach-back is therefore close to the length of the whole trajectory. This is why reach-back correlates so strongly with prompt length (Spearman rank correlation ρ = 0.94; Appendix D.3). Each of the 62 operators with defined reach-back tests exactly one primary skill, and most operators use single radius level. Reach-back, impact radius, primary skill, and output length are therefore correlated by construction (Appendix D.3). A.4 SOURCES OF IMPACT RADIUS LABELS Section 3 defines the four radius levels. When we measure the level of an item, we compute it from the execution diff of the final action. This diff is the difference between the state before the action runs and the state after it. An empty diff gives L0. diff that changes only entities that the action names gives L1 if it changes one of them and L2 if it changes two or more, and diff that changes any entity the action does not name gives L3. Table 8 gives the number of items at each level and their pooled success, separately for levels measured in this way and levels declared by the operator that built the item. Pooled success is the share of passing decisions over all 20 models, where decision is one models scored answer on one item. All 552 L0 items have measured radius, and 153 of the 155 items whose gold is an error are at L0. The 32 Side-Effect Propagation items, which are post-action probes, follow different rule. In each of them, the scored final action is read that follows the last action of the prefix and checks the state after it. Each of these items carries the radius of that last prefix action instead of the radius of the read. That action changes the state in 28 of the items and changes nothing in the other 4, which are at L0. These items have no reach-back. Finally, 11 items have no radius. Their pooled success is 55.00% (121 of 220 decisions, from 11 items and 20 models). Not every label comes from an execution diff  (Table 8)  . The other labels are declared by an operator, and they have two sources. First, the synthetic long-horizon audits are labeled L3 by construction. An audits answer depends on state from many parts of the world, but we do not read its level from diff. These audits account for 945 of the 953 declared L3 items. Second, the operator for cross-file build reconciliation assigns L1, L2, and L3 in rotation by surface index. It produces the other 8 declared L3 items and all 30 declared L1 and L2 items (15 each). Its 38 labels do not describe the state change that the action makes. The L1 and L2 rates in Section 6.1 include them, and Table 8 reports measured and declared labels separately. On the 638 items with measured radius, success shows no steady trend with the radius level (43.49%, 49.17%, 36.93%, and 51.88% from L0 to L3), although L1, L2, and L3 hold only 18, 44, and 24 such items. The low pooled success at L3 (5.10%) comes instead from the 953 declared L3 items, which pass at 3.92%. Radius, reach-back, and operator are also closely tied to one another. Of the 966 L3 items with defined reach-back, 952 have reach-back of more than 40 turns. Table 8: Impact radius labels by how they were assigned. These gates decide whether an item can be scored at all, and they are separate from the metrics we use to score the responses of the subject models. Some gates are deterministic, such as the gates that every fact in the gold also appears in the prefix and that each constraint item raises the expected error. sections.title: B EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 MODELS AND SERVING Each prompt holds one system instruction, the items history, and its final action, with no solved examples from other items, so the evaluation is zero-shot. Every history already shows at least six 19 earlier observations from the same environment. Prompts are also long. For GPT-6 Astra, the median item takes 26,813 prompt tokens and the longest takes 131,894. We do not test few-shot or many-shot prompting. We include two Qwen 3.8 models. Qwen 3.8 Max is Qwens flagship model (Alibaba Group, 2026), and Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is cost-efficient model with new architecture (Qwen Team, 2026). Max scores higher (25.31% vs. 23.22%) but does not solve superset of Flash Nexts items. Flash Next passes 112 items that Max fails, and Max passes 146 that Flash Next fails. We run each general-purpose LLM at the high reasoning setting that its provider supports. GPT-6 Astra is queried through the OpenAI API, and GPT-6 Sol through OpenRouter with OpenAI pinned as the provider. We serve Qwen 3.8 Flash Next ourselves, with thinking on and the chat templates reasoning effort set to xhigh. We sample it at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and top-k 20. For QwenAgentWorld we follow its published sampling recipe (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, thinking on), and we use the same sampling parameters for DWM. Our harness sends each trajectory to the model as an OpenAI-compatible conversation, with the gold withheld. For every request we log the providers response, the visible text, and the tool calls. We also log token usage, the finish reason, latency, the reasoning settings, and any errors. We send each model one primary request per item, and we never resample usable primary response, since drawing again until response passes would inflate models score. We release every response and judge record, so every score can be recomputed without querying model again. We report 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from bootstrap over items: we redraw the items with replacement 2,000 times, recompute the score on each redrawn set, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles (Appendix D). Because each model answers each item once, these intervals reflect only the choice of items and leave out the variation between repeated responses to the same item. No models interval is wider than 4.96 points, the widest being GPT-6 Astras (47.0652.02%). GPT-6 Astra leads the runner-up, Grok 4.6, by 350 items, or 21.45 points (95% CI 19.12 to 23.77). We retry request only when it fails at the provider, returns no visible answer, or reaches its output limit without an answer. We call such retry recovered request. The settings above apply to the primary requests, and some recovered requests used different ones. The 73 recovered requests for Qwen-AgentWorld and the 36 for DWM all ran with thinking off and without top-k, and one of the 36 DWM requests used greedy decoding. For five general-purpose LLMs, some recovered requests ran below the high reasoning setting. Of these, 374 were for Gemini 3.7 Flash, 17 for Inkling, and 3 for Qwen 3.8 Max, all at low effort. Another 233 were for GLM 5.3, at low or minimal effort or with thinking disabled, and one was for Laguna S2.1, with reasoning disabled. None of these 628 lower-effort requests produced passing answer. B.2 REFUSALS AND NON-RESPONSES Of the 32,640 modelitem pairs, 28,854 (88.40%) have usable response. The other 3,786 have none. Of these, 3,696 are provider refusals, all from four Claude models. The remaining 90 are completions that were still empty or errored after recovery. Claude Opus 5.5 refused 675 items (41.36% of its items), and Claude Fable 5.1 refused 668 (40.93%). The other two refused more. Claude Opus 5 refused 1,044 items (63.97%), and Claude Fable 5 refused 1,309 (80.21%). Claude Fable 5.1 also accounts for most of the empty or errored completions, 82 of the 90. The rest are 4 from Claude Opus 5, 3 from Claude Opus 5.5, and 1 from Qwen 3.8 Flash Next. None of the 90 contains visible answer. In 86 of them, the model used its whole output budget of 65,536 tokens without producing one (finish reason length). Of the other four, two Claude Opus 5 responses have no finish reason, third ended with provider error, and the Qwen 3.8 Flash Next response ended normally with only blank lines. Of the 90, 89 are synthetic long-horizon audits with declared L3 label (Appendix A.4), and their reach-backs run from 477 to 1,200 turns (median 720). For the four models with empty or errored completions, the retry repeated the request exactly, with the same model, provider, prompt, reasoning setting, and output budget. We did not retry with larger output budget. We count response as refusal when the provider ends it with content-filter stop reason (finish_reason = content_filter). We do not use the answer text to decide whether 20 model refused. response that ends this way counts as refusal even when it carries partial text. Of the 24 refusals with partial text, 21 come from Claude Opus 5.5 and one from each of the other three refusing models. We score refusals as failures, since simulator that declines to produce an observation cannot be used in rollout. The 90 empty or errored completions also count as failures. Both groups stay in every models denominator, so task success measures usable simulation. Each refusal also carries Anthropics stated reason, and Anthropics native stop reason is refusal in every case. For 3,674 of the 3,696 refusals (99.40%), the request triggered restrictions on violative cyber content: 672 of 675 for Claude Opus 5.5, 661 of 668 for Claude Fable 5.1, all 1,044 for Claude Opus 5, and 1,297 of 1,309 for Claude Fable 5. The other 22 cite Anthropics terms on reverse engineering or duplicating model outputs. The cyber blocks come from Anthropics cyber safeguards, safety classifiers that stop requests that could enable cyber harm, such as malware or exploit development. To keep safety margin, these classifiers can also block benign work, such as general IT administration (Anthropic, 2026f;g). The stated reason names only the policy area, so we cannot tell which content in an item triggered block. Every refused response came from the requested model, with no fallback to another model. Refusals are more common on some kinds of items than on others. By domain, Claude Fable 5.1 refused 374 of the 526 Code items but only 11 of the 334 Games items, and Claude Opus 5.5 refused 295 Code items and 53 Games items (compare their success by domain in Table 21). Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 also refused more often when the reach-back was long. Claude Opus 5 refused 72.6% of the items beyond 40 turns but 40.7% of those within 40 turns. For Claude Fable 5, the two rates are 84.5% and 68.1%. In contrast, Claude Fable 5.1 refused 40.9% on both sides, and Claude Opus 5.5 refused 42.4% and 39.0%. The higher refusal rates of Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 at long reach-back slightly widen the pooled gap between short and long reach-back. If we removed refusals from each models denominator, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 would score 44.93% and 44.22%, and Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Fable 5 would score 36.62% and 36.84%. Among the error-outcome items, whose executed action returns an error or block (Appendix D.6), Claude Opus 5.5 would pass 96.81% (91 of 94) of those it answered, and Claude Fable 5.1 would pass 98.77% (80 of 81). However, these rates depend on which items each model chose to answer, so they cannot be compared with the scores of the other models. Of the 28,854 usable responses from all 20 models, 22.26% pass. Finally, we repeated the comparisons within groups of similar items from Appendix D.3 without the four refusing models. These comparisons group the items by primary skill, or by the operator that generated them. In each group they take the difference in success between items beyond and within 40 turns of reach-back, and they average these differences over the groups, giving more weight to groups with more items on both sides (the MantelHaenszel difference). Without the refusing models, the conclusions do not change. Within skill, items beyond 40 turns still score 26.67 points lower than items within 40 turns (95% CI 29.63 to 23.71). Within operator, the gap disappears (+2.72 points, 95% CI 1.05 to 6.58). B.3 HYBRID GRADING The grader first applies the deterministic metrics in Table 10. Each items scoring contract, which comes from the executable environment, sets which comparisons apply, such as whether order matters and which numeric tolerance holds. metric passes response when it shows that the response and the gold are equivalent: the same text after whitespace is normalized, the same parsed structure, the same numbers within tolerance, or the same error class and referent. metric fails response when it finds contradiction: parsed value or referenced entity that differs from the gold, required field or side effect that is missing or an unsupported one that is invented, success reported for an action that fails or an error for one that succeeds, or broken order that the task requires. response that no metric settles, such as game outcome stated in other words, goes to the LLM judge (Appendix B.4). Table 10 also shows how prior evaluations cover each metric. Six of the eight come from earlier world-model evaluations or from standard practice, and to our knowledge separate deterministic check of the error class is new. Our primary result is binary task success under the frozen hybrid grader. We treat the results by domain, skill, reach-back, and radius as diagnostic slices. B.4 JUDGE CONFIGURATION We use GPT-5.6 Terra in two roles. As the validity judge, it checks whether an items executed gold follows uniquely from the history and final action that the model sees. As the response judge, it decides the responses that the deterministic metrics cannot settle. If Terra response judgment is missing, malformed, uncertain, or below the confidence threshold, GPT-5.6 Sol judges the response again with the same prompt. Both judges run at temperature 0 with seed 0 and low reasoning effort  (Table 11)  . Each judgment reports the judges own confidence (Prompt D), and both judges accept judgment only when this confidence is at least 0.80. Response calls have an output budget of 16,384 tokens. The response judge records semantic correctness and format compliance separately, and only semantic correctness counts toward task success. harmless wrapper around correct answer may therefore fail format compliance without changing the verdict. GPT-5.6 Sol is also one of the models we evaluate, and both judges come from the same provider as four other evaluated models, including the leader, GPT-6 Astra. For this reason we blind the judge. It does not see which model wrote the response or the metadata of the operator that generated the item. It also does not see the deterministic decision or another judges answer. We compared both judges with provisional adjudications of 130 boundary examples. Terra matched 103 of them (79.2%) and disagreed on 27. Sol matched 97 (74.6%) and disagreed on 33. The two judges agreed with each other on 96.2% of the 1,570 responses that both scored. Some of their disagreements with the adjudications came from errors about tool semantics. We therefore let the deterministic metrics decide whenever they can, and we keep Sol as the fallback. In second comparison, on 131 provisionally adjudicated decisions, Terra matched 113 (86.3%) and the best Gemini configuration we tried matched 86 (65.6%), so we did not replace Terra with Gemini judge. Because Sol is also one of the evaluated models, we checked 59 labeled cases in which Sol wrote the response. sections.title: C QUALITY AUDIT
sections.content: C.1 HUMAN EVALUATION We recruited six industry experts through Upwork, each with computer science degree and experience with tool-calling agents. The experts worked independently, and each rated 100 of the 200 sampled items on five-point Likert scale. The next state they rated is each items gold, which we obtain by execution, although the guidelines below call it the predicted next state. The study therefore rates the benchmarks answers rather than model outputs. All six rated the same 80 anchor items, which we use to measure agreement, the share of annotator pairs that give an item the same score  (Table 3)  . Each expert also rated 20 of the other 120 items, which widens coverage to 200 items at 100 ratings per expert. Of the 80 anchor items, the 78 that are in the release cover all five domains (34 Code, 20 Enterprise, 9 Dialogue, 8 Math and Science, and 7 Games items) and all 19 skills. Sixty of them are L0 and 6 are L3, whereas 977 of the 1,632 items in the corpus are L3. Their median reach-back is 101 turns and their longest is 600, against median of 240 and maximum of 1,680 in the corpus. The anchor set therefore contains few of the synthetic long-horizon audits, which make up 945 of the 977 L3 items (Appendix A.4). The LLM extension in Appendix C.2 rates 1,627 of the 1,632 items and so also covers these audits. Each item was rated from 1 to 5 on four dimensions  (Table 12)  . State Coherence asks whether the predicted state is consistent with everything established in the prefix, with no contradictions and no invented entities. Interface Realism asks whether the output matches the real systems structure, schema, error format, and field values. Outcome Correctness asks whether the predicted state reflects the correct outcome of the action. Finally, Constraint Enforcement asks whether an illegal or unauthorized action fails correctly. When the final action was valid, annotators marked this dimension as not applicable. In comments beyond their ratings, the annotators noted that the next states they rated showed strong adherence to constraints, and they suggested that generating trajectories by execution gives reliable signal for evaluating models. The two issues they raised most often were incorrect error reasoning and doubt about whether long trajectories with many distractor turns give reliable signal. Each annotator first completed five qualification items without AI assistance. The main task then proceeded in two steps. Annotators rated State Coherence and Interface Realism before the expected output was shown to them, and once it was revealed they rated Outcome Correctness and Constraint Enforcement. The 200-item sample was also checked for personally identifying, sensitive, and harmful content. We reproduce the annotation guidelines below, and Table 12 gives the rubric.

sections.content: Annotator Requirements Before beginning, confirm you meet all of the following. If you do not meet any, do not proceed and notify the project coordinator. Technical background: familiar with tool-calling LLMs, tool schemas, and how an environment responds to an action. Education and experience: CS degree; experience using and building AI agents. Hands-on fluency in at least two of: Linux/Bash and filesystem semantics, SQL/relational databases, REST APIs and JSON schemas, HTTP-status/errno error semantics; that is, you can say what command, query, or call returns (and the correct error) without running it. Age: at least 18 years of age. Overview of Tasks You will complete one annotation task with 100 items. Each item is JSON-formatted conversation ending in an action; you rate the predicted next state. Qualification Task (complete first) Before the full dataset, complete short qualification task of 5 sample items (provided by the coordinator). Complete them independently, without rushing. We call each model-item pair decision, so slice of items has 20n decisions, and pooled success on the slice is the percentage of its decisions that pass. Because every model is scored on every item, pooled success equals the mean of the 20 per-model rates. We round percentages half-up. Our 95% intervals come from bootstrap over items, which shows how much pooled rate would change if the benchmark held different sample of items. We resample the items of slice 2,000 times with fixed seed. Each resample draws as many items as the slice holds, uniformly and with replacement, and keeps all 20 models decisions on every drawn item. The interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the pooled rates over the 2,000 resamples. Differences between rates are in percentage points, which we call points. When we rerun the bootstrap with 20 different seeds, the 20 values of each interval endpoint lie within 0.18 points of one another for the pooled rate over all 1,632 items, and within 1.67 points for the 33 L1 items. D.1 DIFFICULTY AND STATE DEPENDENCY Reach-back is the number of turns between the final action and the earlier event that its answer depends on. Impact radius has four levels: at L0 the action changes no state, at L1 and L2 it changes only entities that it names (one at L1, two or more at L2), and at L3 it changes at least one entity that it does not name (Section 3). Table 14 gives pooled success by reach-back band and by impact radius, and Table 15 gives both breakdowns for each model. From L2 to L3 it drops by another 22.44 points (15.73 to 28.99). Between L1 and L2, however, it barely changes. D.3 COMPARISONS WITHIN SKILL AND OPERATOR This section asks whether success still falls with reach-back, or with impact radius, when we compare only similar items. Among items with the same primary skill, both gaps remain. Among items made by the same operator, the reach-back gap disappears and the L3L0 gap reverses. The comparisons within operator, however, can use only the operators that make items on both sides: 21 of the 62 operators for reach-back and 5 for radius. Reach-back is hard to study on its own, because it varies with other properties of an item. When we group items by operator, the differences between the group means account for 81.64% of the variance in log(1 + reach-back). The share is 61.78% when we group by radius, 37.41% by primary skill, and 9.87% by domain. Each share is η2, the squared correlation ratio defined in Appendix D.2, for that grouping. For primary skill it corresponds to η = 0.61 there (0.612 0.37). Items with long reach-back also have long prompts and, to lesser degree, long gold outputs. The Spearman rank correlation ρ, the correlation between the items ranks on two quantities, is 0.94 between reach-back and prompt length and 0.67 between reach-back and gold length. We therefore compare items only within groups (strata) that share property, such as the same skill or the same operator. In each group, we take the difference in success between items beyond and within 40 turns, or between L3 and L0 items. We then average these differences over the groups. group with n0 items on one side and n1 on the other gets weight n0n1/(n0 + n1), which is large only when the group has many items on both sides, and group with items on only one side gets no weight. This weighted average is the MantelHaenszel risk difference. Because each gap compares items from the same group, differences between groups, such as one skill being harder than another, do not enter it. We compute it on decision counts, so each item contributes its 20 model decisions. For the 95% interval, we resample items with replacement 2,000 times within each group and side, keeping all 20 decisions of each item. Of the 62 operators, only 21 have items on both sides of 40 turns. Table 17 gives both differences. Each row uses one grouping, from single group holding all items (the raw gap) to finer groupings. To do so, we fit quasi-binomial regression, which is logistic regression whose variance may exceed the binomial variance. Its outcome is the share of the 20 models that pass an item, and its predictors are the items domain, radius level, reach-back band (the bands of Table 14, plus one for items without reach-back), and outcome type (error or normal; Appendix D.6). domains adjusted rate is the average predicted success over all 1,632 items when every item is assigned to that domain.
